newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP to make statement on Ok Tedi mine.
newsitem.headline: BHP to make statement on Ok Tedi mine.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd expects to issue a statement later on Thursday about operations at the Ok Tedi copper mine in Papua New Guinea, which has been unable to deliver concentrates to port because of dry river conditions, a BHP spokesman said.
BHP barges copper from the mine to Port Moresby Harbour on the Fly River, but the river level is now too low for the barges.
Storage of copper concentrates at the port have run dry, BHP said on June 6.
"At this stage there certainly is no talk of force majeure, although there could be some rearrangement of shipping schedules," the spokesman said.
BHP has held discussions with Japanese customers over delaying shipments of around 25,000 tonnes until conditions improve, he said.
"We haven't cancelled any shipments as far as the customer is concerned," the spokesman said.
"We've had somebody in Japan talking to them about rescheduling shipments because there was a vessel on time charter waiting to load and there is nothing there," he said.
Ok Tedi normally ships about 50,000 tonnes of concentrate each month, mostly to smelting companies in Asia and Europe.

However, there currently is insufficient water in the shipping channel to allow a fleet of specially-built shallow draft barges, each capable of carrying 25,000 tonnes of concntrates, to ply the full length of the Fly River from the Port of Kiunga.

Concentrates are transported by pipeline from the mine to the port of Kiunga, and then by barge down the Fly River for loading onto a silo vessel in the Gulf of Papua before being transferred to bulk carriers.
BHP said earlier this month the mine was preparing contingency plans to reduce milling of ore starting around June 12 if conditions failed to improve.
At the time BHP said mining operations would be able to continue, concentrating on removal of ore waste.
Ok Tedi is 52.6 percent owned by BHP, with Canada's Inmet Mining Corp owning 17.4 percent and the rest held by the Papua New Guinea government.
